blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A team reuses its Visa link's packager, unchanged, for a new link whose specification writes every digit, length and text character as one EBCDIC byte and the bitmap as 8 binary bytes. The Visa packager already writes its text fields in EBCDIC. What does the new host make of the team's first message?

options.text: It can't read the MTI, since the MTI's four digits arrive packed into two bytes
options.says: 6.1: a BCD packager writes the MTI as 01 00, and an EBCDIC host takes the first four bytes, 01 00 70 20, for the MTI

options.text: It can't read the MTI, since the MTI's four digits arrive as ASCII characters
options.says: 6.1: unit 5's Visa packager writes digits in BCD, two to a byte, not as ASCII characters; the MTI is 01 00

options.text: It reads the MTI but not the amount, since the amount's twelve digits arrive packed into six bytes
options.says: 6.1: the MTI is numeric too, so the BCD packager writes it as two bytes

options.text: It reads the MTI but not the terminal, since the terminal's eight characters arrive as ASCII bytes
options.says: 6.1: the Visa packager already writes text in EBCDIC; its BCD numbers, the MTI first, are what the host can't read

origin.section: 6.1. A Mastercard Message Is EBCDIC Characters Behind a Binary Bitmap

questions.stem: A packager file for an EBCDIC link declares field 42 with the wrong class, one that writes ASCII. The team's test packs an 0100 with field 42 set, unpacks the bytes with the same file, and compares every field. What does the test report?

options.text: It fails on field 42, since the unpacked value differs from the value the test set
options.says: 6.2: one class packs and unpacks the field, so the value comes back unchanged

options.text: It fails on field 42, since the packed bytes differ from the bytes the link expects
options.says: 6.2: a round trip never compares with the link's bytes; only a sample comparison does

options.text: It passes, since the unpacked value equals the value the test set
options.says: 6.2: the same wrong class packs and unpacks, so a round trip passes; only sample bytes catch it

options.text: It passes, since the packed bytes equal the bytes the link expects
options.says: 6.2: field 42 goes out in ASCII where the link expects EBCDIC; the test passes for another reason

origin.section: 6.2. A Packager That Reads Its Own Messages Back Proves Nothing

questions.stem: A client puts four ASCII digits in front of each message. The host it connects to expects a binary length in front of each message, as PostChannel writes it. The client sends a 58-byte 0100. What does the host do?

options.text: It reads a length of 12336 and waits for more bytes, since it takes the first two digits as the length
options.says: 6.3: 30 30 is 12336 as a binary length, so the host waits for bytes that never come until its timeout

options.text: It reads a length of 58 and waits for more bytes, since it takes all four digits as the length
options.says: 6.3: a binary-length host reads two bytes, 30 30, as 12336; it never reads the four digits as 58

options.text: It reads a length of 12336 and refuses the frame, since it takes the first two digits as the length
options.says: 6.3: the host can't know how many bytes are still coming, so it waits until its read timeout

options.text: It reads a length of 58 and refuses the frame, since it takes all four digits as the length
options.says: 6.3: a binary-length host reads two bytes, 30 30, as 12336, and it waits instead of refusing

origin.section: 6.3. A Frame Is a Two-Byte Binary Length, Then the Message

questions.stem: Your packager declares field 48 with MasterCardEBCDICSubFieldPackager and the three subelement tags your application uses. A network release starts sending a new tag, 27, in field 48 of every authorization response. What happens on release day?

options.text: Responses fail to unpack at field 48, since the packager refuses any undefined tag
options.says: 6.4: the subfield packager refuses an undeclared tag, and the whole message with it

options.text: Responses fail to unpack at field 48, since the packager looks for each tag at a fixed offset
options.says: 6.4: the packager finds each tag where it is; fixed offsets are the hand-written reader's mistake, and that reader misreads without failing

options.text: Responses unpack with the extra subelement dropped, since the packager steps over any undefined tag
options.says: 6.4: stepping over unknown tags is what a reader must do, but jPOS's subfield packager refuses them unless every tag is declared

options.text: Responses unpack with the other subelements misread, since the packager looks for each tag at a fixed offset
options.says: 6.4: the packager finds each tag where it is; the fixed-offset reader is the other way to fail

origin.section: 6.4. Field 48 Is Read Tag by Tag, and an Unknown Tag Must Not Stop the Message

concepts: A packager borrowed from a BCD link with only its text fields switched to EBCDIC still sends a BCD MTI the host can't read.
The frame is a two-byte binary length and the message; a binary-length host reading ASCII digits waits for 12336 bytes until its read timeout.
jPOS's subfield packager refuses a tag it has no definition for, and the whole message with it, so every tag is declared or the field is split in code.
